result:
I keep coming back to lichen.

For most of the time humans have named things, lichen was filed as a plant—a scrappy, slow, unglamorous one, the gray-green crust on gravestones and the orange freckles on granite. Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that sounded almost indecent: lichen wasn't one organism at all. It was a fungus and an alga living so entangled that they had become a single body with a single shape, a shape neither could make alone. His colleagues were furious. It offended a tidy idea of what an individual was.

He was right, of course. And more recently researchers found a third partner hiding in many lichens—a yeast nobody had noticed for a century and a half, because nobody was looking for it. The thing on the rock is a small committee.

What I like is how patient the whole arrangement is. Lichens grow perhaps a millimeter a year. Some individuals on Arctic stone are thought to be several thousand years old, older than the alphabet used to describe them. They colonize bare rock where nothing else can hold on, secrete faint acids, and over centuries crumble that rock into the first thin soil. Forests eventually stand on the leftovers of their work.

There's something steadying in that. A partnership so complete it passed as a single being, quietly turning stone into ground, asking for nothing but rain and light and a very long time.
